questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a first moment depends on the placement of mass
questions.stem: Explain why the first moment of a body about a line depends on where the mass sits, and not only on how much mass there is.

answer.exemplar: A first moment about a chosen line is the sum over the body of each piece's mass multiplied by its perpendicular distance from that line. Two bodies with the same total mass can therefore have very different first moments, because moving mass nearer or further from the line changes the weighted distance that gets summed. This is exactly why the first moment is the right tool for locating a balance point, and why a second moment, which weights distance twice, describes resistance to turning.

questions.explanation: A good answer defines the first moment as mass times perpendicular distance from the line, summed, and notes that equal mass can give different moments. Mentioning the second moment adds contrast.
questions.hint: Mass times perpendicular distance from the line.

questions.stem: A counterweight consists of a 6 kilogram block whose centre is 0.4 metres above the table and a 2 kilogram block whose centre is 1.0 metre above the table. What is the vertical coordinate of the combined centre of mass?

options.text: 0.70 metres, the plain average of the two heights 0.4 and 1.0 metres
options.misconception: averages the two heights without weighting by the masses

options.text: 0.40 metres, since the heavier block dominates the combined assembly
options.misconception: assumes the heavier block drags the centre to its own level

1.00 metres, since the upper block sets the top of the whole stack
options.misconception: takes the highest part of the stack as the combined centre

questions.explanation: The combined centre of mass is the mass-weighted mean of the two heights, so 6 times 0.4 plus 2 times 1.0 over 8 gives 0.55 m. A plain average ignores the weights, and neither extreme is the mean.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Moment of inertia of a disk
questions.learningObjective: Derive the disk inertia about perpendicular and in-plane axes
questions.stem: Explain in a field notebook why a solid disk of mass M and radius R has moment of inertia M R squared over 2 about its central axis, and about M R squared over 4 about an axis in its plane.

answer.exemplar: Each ring of radius r and thickness dr has mass dM proportional to r dr, and it sits at distance r from the central axis. Integrating r squared times r dr from 0 to R gives a factor of one quarter of the total mass times R squared, which is M R squared over 2 for the axis perpendicular to the face. For an axis lying in the plane, each ring contributes half of its r squared moment because the ring is symmetric about that line, which gives M R squared over 4.

questions.explanation: A good answer notes that rings of mass proportional to r dr sit at distance r, so integrating r cubed gives M R squared over 2. It should explain that an in-plane axis collects half of each ring.
questions.hint: Build the disk from thin rings.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: Describe the coordinate method for finding a triangle centroid
questions.stem: Describe, for a notebook entry, how you would find the centroid of a triangular region whose three vertices are given as coordinates, and why that method works for any triangle.

answer.exemplar: Add the three x coordinates and divide by three to get the centroid's x value, and do the same for the y coordinates. This works because the centroid of a uniform triangle is the average of its vertices: a triangle can be split into three equal-area pieces, each of which has one vertex in common, and each piece's own centroid lies two thirds of the way along the median from that vertex. Averaging the three vertices therefore matches the point where the medians meet, for scalene, right and obtuse triangles alike.

questions.explanation: A good answer says the centroid is the coordinatewise average of the vertices and explains that each median runs two thirds from its vertex. It should note the rule holds for every triangle.
questions.hint: Average the coordinates of the three vertices.

questions.stem: A folded cardboard box in the log has a heavy roll of tape in the bottom corner and empty flaps above. How should the box's centre of mass height be estimated?

options.text: As the geometric centre of the box, since the tape is small and can be ignored
options.misconception: ignores a small but heavy item because it takes little space

options.text: As the centre of the heaviest single component, ignoring everything else in the box
options.misconception: takes the heaviest component's centre as the whole centre

options.text: As the mass-weighted average of the tape's centre height and the cardboard's centre height
As the centre of the empty flaps, since they occupy the largest volume
options.misconception: weighs components by volume rather than by mass

questions.explanation: A composite body's centre of mass is the mass-weighted average of its parts' centres, so the tape pulls the result down only in proportion to its mass. A small heavy item cannot be ignored.
questions.hint: Weight each component's centre by its mass.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: Obtain slab mass and first moment in two stages
questions.stem: Two stages are needed: first the total mass of a uniform rectangular plate 5 metres by 2 metres with density 3 kilograms per square metre, then its first moment about the edge that runs along the 5 metre side.

options.text: Mass 30 kilograms and first moment 150 kilogram metres, using the full 5 m distance
options.misconception: multiplies mass by the full length, not the mean distance

options.text: Mass 30 kilograms and first moment 75 kilogram metres, since the mean distance is 2.5 m
Mass 15 kilograms and first moment 75 kilogram metres, forgetting the plate's width
options.misconception: drops one of the two edge lengths when computing the mass

options.text: Mass 30 kilograms and first moment 60 kilogram metres, using half the plate's mass
options.misconception: halves the mass without any physical reason for doing so

questions.explanation: Mass is length times width times density, giving 30 kg, and the mean distance from the 5 m edge is 2.5 m, so the first moment is 75 kg m. Using the full length would double it.
questions.hint: Find the mass, then multiply by the mean distance.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Centre of mass of a varying-density plate
questions.learningObjective: Reject an invalid criterion for locating a centre of mass
questions.stem: A log entry claims the centre of mass of a plate is where the areal density equals its average value. What is wrong with that claim?

options.text: The centre of mass is the density-weighted mean height, not the height where density equals its average
Nothing is wrong, since a density profile is uniquely determined by its average
options.misconception: believes the mean density fixes the whole density profile

options.text: The claim reverses the roles, because the average density fixes the centre instead
options.misconception: reverses the relation between density profile and centre

options.text: The claim is valid only for plates whose density is constant from base to top
options.misconception: restricts the rule to constant density only

questions.explanation: The centre of mass divides the first moment by the total mass, weighting each height by the local density, so it is a weighted mean rather than a level where density matches its average.
questions.hint: Weight heights by the local density.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: Check the units claimed for a first moment
questions.stem: A reviewer reads a log entry that claims a first moment has units of kilograms and says this proves mass and moment are the same kind of quantity. How should the reviewer respond?

options.text: The entry is right, because moment and mass differ only by the choice of units
options.misconception: treats the unit difference as a mere naming preference

options.text: The entry is wrong, since a first moment should have units of kilograms per metre
options.misconception: claims the correct units are mass per unit length

options.text: The entry cannot be judged, because units for a moment have never been agreed
options.misconception: asserts that the units of a moment are undefined or unagreed

options.text: The entry is wrong, since a first moment carries units of kilograms times metres, not kilograms alone

questions.explanation: A first moment sums mass times distance, so its units are kilograms times metres and it is a different kind of quantity from mass. The difference is not a convention, and it is not mass per length.
questions.hint: Mass times distance is the dimension of a moment.
